about.title: About Me
about.description: Hi, I’m Arda Güner. I started with C++ and today I build projects across web, mobile and game development.
detailedDescription: Hello, I’m Arda Güner. I started my software development journey with C++, and the grounding it gave me in algorithms and memory management still shapes how I approach every new technology. Over time I moved into modern web technologies and built a strong technical foundation there. I develop sustainable, high-performance, user-focused web applications with the JavaScript ecosystem — React, TypeScript and Node.js in particular — as well as Next.js and ASP.NET Core. I see software not just as a job, but as a continuously evolving problem-solving discipline.

These days my focus is on game development: desktop game projects in Python and Delphi, and mobile and web games with Godot 4 and Phaser 3 + Matter.js. On mobile I build user-friendly, scalable applications with Flutter and Dart, and use Capacitor to bring my web-based games to mobile platforms. I’m also actively learning Kotlin and continually working to deepen my technical expertise on mobile platforms.

In the past, I worked as a coding and computer science instructor, helping children develop algorithmic thinking and problem-solving skills. In Scratch-based workshops, my focus was not only on teaching how to code, but on building systematic thinking, step-by-step reasoning, and a creative, productive mindset.
Alongside these, I solo-develop independent (indie) games under my own game studio, Ardeko Studios, bringing my creative concepts and gaming passions to life.

apex.title: How one invisible HTTP header
apex.lede: Online mode looked fine. Until two people joined. The bug was not that the code ran wrong — it was that it silently never ran at all.

meta.v: None — each client owns only its own car

p: With two people in the same room the race never started properly. The host counted down from 3; the second player counted down from 10, sometimes 11. Worse, players could not see each other — and it was one-sided: one saw the other, the other did not.
That asymmetry was the useful clue. A plain connectivity problem would have hurt both sides equally.
To keep countdowns and lap times consistent, clients locked onto server time. The lock was done like this:
after: `Date` is not on the CORS safelisted response header list, and Firebase RTDB does not send `Access-Control-Expose-Headers`. So in the browser `res.headers.get('date')` always returns null; the function exited on its first line and `clockOffset` stayed 0 forever.
I confirmed it with curl: the response does carry a `Date` header, but no `Access-Control-Expose-Headers`. The server sends it, the browser hides it.

p: Once every client was using its own raw wall clock, two things broke at once.
**Countdown:** the host writes `raceStartAt = ownClock + 4000`. A client whose clock is 8 seconds behind computes `raceStartAt − ownClock = 12000` and starts counting from 12.

**Visibility:** the stale-player check is `now − p.ts > 6000`. Timestamps were written with local clocks too, so the error had a direction: a behind-clock player's timestamp looked 8 seconds old to everyone else and got dropped from rendering, while in the other direction the difference went negative and passed. That is where the asymmetry came from.
Instead of an unreadable header, use the database's own server timestamp. Writing `{".sv":"timestamp"}` to RTDB returns the resolved server time in the response.
after: The pleasant part: the game already wrote its own `players/<uid>` node every 220 ms. Attaching the sentinel to that write means every sync yields a free clock sample — no extra request.
As a side effect every `ts` in the database now comes from one clock, so the staleness check became symmetric on its own.

p: Three clients were simulated: one with a correct clock, one 8 seconds behind, one 5 seconds ahead — 13 seconds apart end to end.
sections.code:
offsets: hostA=78ms   joinB=8065ms   joinC=-4939ms
hostA: countdown 3 (2865ms)
joinB: countdown 3 (2877ms)
joinC: countdown 3 (2882ms)
after: All three count from 3, within 17 milliseconds of each other. On the staleness side each sees the others as roughly 250 ms old, against a 6000 ms threshold.

p: This bug made no noise. `if (!h) return;` throws nothing and logs nothing; the code worked, it just did nothing.

It was also invisible in single-client testing: on one machine the clock offset is zero, so a broken sync behaves exactly like a working one. The failure needs a second machine — and a second machine whose clock has drifted.

The lesson: when you read a value that comes from outside, the "could not read it" branch should not be a silent early return. It should complain at least once, because you cannot tell a broken sync from an absent one without measuring.

apex.ctaText: Open the same room code in two tabs; both will count down from 3 together.
